label: L17
title: Multi-modal Artificial Intelligence and its applications
brief: Doctors, agronomists and hurricane forecasters all decide from several data types at once (images, text, tabular records, time series), so the lecture asks whether machines can do the same. HAIM (Holistic AI in Medicine, Nature Digital Medicine 2022) turns each modality of a patient record (notes, X-rays, ECG reports, chart and lab events) into embeddings and combines them into one unified patient representation; on 34,537 MIMIC-IV ICU records it beats single-modality models by 6-33% across mortality, diagnosis and length-of-stay targets. The same approach is deployed at Hartford HealthCare (7 hospitals), where calibrated discharge, destination, mortality and ICU models drive daily green/yellow alerts and outperform doctors' estimated discharge dates. A preliminary treatment-vs-control comparison shows a 0.67-day length-of-stay reduction, which the lecture converts into about $35.9M of annual contribution margin. A second case, multimodal hurricane forecasting, combines storm time series, reanalysis maps and past forecasts to match the best NHC models and improve the official consensus forecast by 5-15%.
kp: Motivation: real decision makers combine modalities (scans, notes, EHR tables, time series, genomics); the human five senses are the analogy.
HAIM fuses notes, X-rays, ECG, admissions info and chart/lab/procedure events into a unified patient representation.
Text (clinical notes, ECG reports, serialized tabular events) is embedded with ClinicalBERT/BioBERT into 768-element vectors.
MIMIC-IV: 34,537 emergency-ICU records from Beth Israel Deaconess; targets are mortality, 10 chest diagnoses, and discharge within 48 hours.
HAIM vs single modality: mortality +11-33%, disease classification +6-22%, length of stay +8-20%.
Adding TabText (tabular data written as text, then embedded) to tabular features improves every target, up to +9.73% for Enter ICU 48hr.
Hartford HealthCare deployment: 7 hospitals, hundreds of daily users, AUC roughly 0.76-0.93, well-calibrated probabilities.
Against doctors' estimated discharge dates: AUC +0.18 to +0.21, more discharges detected, precision +10-12%.
LOS fell 0.67 days in 15 fully deployed units (parallel-trend comparison, preliminary), about $35.9M CM per year; $50.8M target with all equivalent units.
Hurricanes: storm time series + reanalysis maps + historical forecasts; competitive with NHC models, improves the NHC consensus by 5-15%.

topics.x: Medical doctors decide using scans, language (reports, notes), tabular EHR data, time series and genomics; agriculture and climate forecasting have the same mix of images, physical measurements and text. The lecture's analogy is the five human senses: multimodality is fundamental to human life, so models should use it too.

HAIM (Soenksen et al., Nature Digital Medicine, 2022) combines notes, X-rays, ECGs, admissions information and chart/lab/procedure events into a single unified patient representation. Unstructured text, including ECG reports and tabular event strings such as 'Troponin T: 0.13 ng/mL, Warning: outside normal', is embedded with ClinicalBERT/BioBERT into a 768-element vector; images go through vision models.

Trained on 34,537 emergency-ICU patient records from Beth Israel Deaconess (chest X-ray, EHR, radiology notes, ECG). Targets are mortality at discharge, 10 chest diagnoses, and discharge within 48 hours. HAIM improves on single-modality models by 11-33% (mortality), 6-22% (diagnosis) and 8-20% (length of stay), and even text-serialized tabular data (TabText) adds lift over plain tabular features.

End-to-end software running daily at 7 hospitals predicts discharge in 24/48 hours, final destination, mortality, and ICU entry/exit in 24/48 hours for physicians, nurses, case and bed managers. AUCs range from about 0.76 to 0.93, predicted probabilities are well calibrated, and simple alert rules (green above 0.5; yellow for a rising 48-hour probability between 0.35 and 0.5) turn scores into action. The models beat doctors' estimated discharge dates on AUC, recall and precision.

Comparing 15 fully deployed units with 12 units without full deployment, and assuming parallel trends, average LOS fell about 0.67 days (flagged as preliminary). The financial chain is patients x LOS reduction = patient-days saved, divided by the new LOS = extra patients that fit, times the backfill share times contribution margin per patient: about $35.9M a year for 15 units and a $50.8M target for all equivalent units.

Boussioux et al. (Weather and Forecasting, 2022) forecast hurricane track and intensity from three sources: historical storm features (time series), reanalysis maps (spatial-temporal vision data) and historical forecast data. At a 24-hour lead time the multimodal model is competitive with the best NHC statistical and dynamical models, and adding it to the operational consensus improves NHC's official forecast by 5-15%.

Current HAIM work covers domestic abuse and human trafficking detection, edema prediction for stroke patients, and early cancer detection from scans, labs and reports; climate uses include precision agriculture, wildfires and weather. The lecture's takeaway is that multimodality is a new paradigm for science, engineering and medicine, and that deep learning is the natural tool for modeling multimodal data.

cards.f: Which data modalities do doctors combine when making decisions (lecture motivation)?
cards.b: Scans (MRI, CT, X-ray), language (radiology reports, doctor and nurse notes), tabular EHR data, time series, and genomic information.
cards.x: The question the lecture poses is whether machines can use the same multimodal mix.

cards.f: What is the human-centric analogy for multimodal AI?
cards.b: The five senses (touch, sight, hearing, smell, taste): multimodality is fundamental to human life, so why not for machines?

cards.f: What does HAIM combine, and into what?
cards.b: Notes, X-rays, ECG, admissions information, and chart/lab/procedure events are combined into a unified patient representation.
cards.x: HAIM = Holistic Artificial Intelligence in Medicine (Nature Digital Medicine, Sept 2022).

cards.f: How does HAIM turn unstructured text (e.g., ECG reports) into model features?
cards.b: With ClinicalBERT/BioBERT embeddings: each text becomes a 768-element vector.
cards.x: The same embedding step is applied to tabular event strings (TabText).

cards.f: What is the TabText idea on the event-string slide?
cards.b: Write time-stamped tabular events as text ('Troponin T: 0.13 ng/mL, Warning: outside normal'), concatenate into a patient summary, and embed it with BioBERT (768-dim).
cards.x: Text carries context such as units and abnormal flags that raw columns lose.

cards.f: MIMIC-IV as used for HAIM: size, source, modalities?
cards.b: 34,537 patient records from emergency ICU rooms at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center; chest X-ray, EHR, radiology notes, ECG.
cards.x: Single hospital source: keep that in mind for generalization.

cards.f: What are HAIM's three target families?
cards.b: Mortality (deceased/hospice vs alive at discharge), diagnosis (10 chest conditions, e.g. pneumonia, edema, cardiomegaly), and length of stay (exit within 48 hours).
cards.x: LOS is framed as a binary classification, not a regression.

cards.f: How much does HAIM improve over single-modality models?
cards.b: Mortality 11-33%, disease classification 6-22%, length of stay 8-20%.
cards.x: Ranges are across the single-modality baselines.

cards.f: What is the 'unexpected result' with TabText?
cards.b: Tabular + TabText beats tabular alone on every target; the largest gains are for ICU entry (+8.40% at 24h, +9.73% at 48h).
cards.x: Gains are relative to the tabular score, e.g. (81.3 - 75)/75 = 8.4%.

cards.f: Hartford HealthCare deployment: scale and what is predicted?
cards.b: 7 hospitals (about 2,500 beds, $5B revenue), hundreds of daily users. Predicts discharge in 24/48h, final destination, mortality, ICU entry/exit in 24/48h.
cards.x: Used to prioritize patients, cut LOS, plan disposition, warn of deterioration and allocate resources.

cards.f: What are the green and yellow discharge alert rules?
cards.b: Green: discharge probability in the next 24h or 48h > 0.5. Yellow: 48h probability between 0.35 and 0.5 AND up by more than 0.1 since yesterday.
cards.x: Yellow needs both the level band and the rising trend.

cards.f: How do the models compare with doctors' estimated discharge dates (EDDs)?
cards.b: AUC +0.18 to +0.21, proportion of discharges detected +1% to +16%, precision +10% to +12% (validated Apr-Oct 2021).
cards.x: Better on ranking, recall and precision at the same time.

cards.f: How was the 0.67-day LOS reduction estimated?
cards.b: 15 units with full deployment after Jan 15, 2023 vs 12 units without full deployment, comparing to a counterfactual under a parallel-trend assumption. Marked preliminary.
cards.x: A difference-in-differences style estimate, not a randomized trial.

cards.f: How does 0.67 days of LOS reduction become $35.9M a year?
cards.b: 49,424 patients x 0.67 = 33,114 patient-days; / 4.98-day new LOS = 6,649 patients' worth of beds; x 50% backfilled = 3,325 extra patients; x $10,796 CM = $35.9M.
cards.x: Adding the 12 control units ($14.9M) gives the $50.8M target.

cards.f: Which three data sources feed the multimodal hurricane model?
cards.b: Historical storm features (time series), reanalysis maps (spatial-temporal vision data), and historical forecast data.

cards.f: What are the key hurricane forecasting results?
cards.b: Performance comparable with the best NHC models; including it in the operational consensus model improves NHC's official forecast by 5-15%.
cards.x: Value comes from adding a different signal to the consensus, not from replacing NHC.

quiz.q: How many patient records from MIMIC-IV does the HAIM study use?
quiz.e: The slide lists 34,537 emergency-ICU records from Beth Israel Deaconess. 49,424 is the yearly patient count in the Hartford financial calculation, a different dataset.

quiz.q: What does ClinicalBERT/BioBERT produce for each text input in HAIM?
o: A 768-element embedding vector
A single risk score between 0 and 1
A bag-of-words count vector
A 10-class diagnosis label
quiz.e: Notes, ECG reports and event strings are each mapped to a 768-element vector that then feeds the unified representation; the embedding is a feature, not a prediction.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three data sources in the multimodal hurricane model?
o: Satellite crop-yield records
Historical storm features (time series)
Reanalysis maps (spatial-temporal data)
Historical forecast data
quiz.e: The three sources are storm time series, reanalysis maps and historical forecasts. Crop yields come up only in the agriculture motivation slide.

quiz.q: How is the length-of-stay target defined in HAIM?
o: Whether the patient exits the hospital within 48 hours
Number of days in hospital (regression)
Whether the patient enters the ICU within 24 hours
Whether the patient is readmitted within 30 days
quiz.e: LOS is a binary target: discharged within 48 hours or not. ICU entry belongs to the TabText comparison and the Hartford models, not to HAIM's LOS target.

quiz.q: When does a patient get a green discharge alert?
o: When the discharge probability in the next 24 or 48 hours exceeds 0.5
When the 48-hour discharge probability is between 0.35 and 0.5
When the mortality probability exceeds 0.5
When the discharge probability rose by more than 0.1 since yesterday
quiz.e: Green means either horizon's discharge probability is above 0.5. The 0.35-0.5 band combined with a >0.1 rise is the yellow rule.

quiz.q: A patient's 48-hour discharge probability was 0.30 yesterday and is 0.44 today; the 24-hour probability is 0.20. Which alert applies?
o: Yellow: 0.44 is in [0.35, 0.5] and rose by 0.14 > 0.1
Green: the 48-hour probability is rising
No alert: neither probability exceeds 0.5
Yellow only if the 24-hour probability is also in [0.35, 0.5]
quiz.e: Yellow needs the 48h probability in 0.35-0.5 and a rise of more than 0.1; both hold (0.44, +0.14). 'No alert' wrongly applies only the green threshold.

quiz.q: For Enter ICU 24hr, tabular scores 75 and tabular + TabText scores 81.3. What relative improvement does the slide report?
quiz.e: (81.3 - 75)/75 = 0.084. 6.3 is the gain in points, not a relative improvement; 7.7% would divide by 81.3 instead of the baseline.

quiz.q: In the TabText table, for which target does TabText alone beat tabular alone by the widest margin?
o: Enter ICU 48hr (72.0 vs 65.8)
Discharge 24hr (73.7 vs 74.6)
Leave ICU 24hr (73.3 vs 73.5)
Discharge 48hr (74.0 vs 74.5)
quiz.e: Enter ICU 48hr gains 6.2 points from TabText alone (next best: Enter ICU 24hr, +2.4). For both discharge targets and Leave ICU 24hr, TabText alone is slightly worse than tabular; it helps there only when combined with tabular.

quiz.q: How was the 0.67-day reduction in length of stay estimated?
o: By comparing 15 fully deployed units with 12 units without full deployment, assuming parallel trends (preliminary)
By a randomized controlled trial across the 7 hospitals
By comparing model predictions with doctors' estimated discharge dates
By simulating discharges from the calibration curve
quiz.e: The slide shows treatment (15 units) vs control (12 units) with a counterfactual line under a parallel-trend assumption, labeled preliminary. The EDD comparison measures prediction quality, not LOS impact.

quiz.q: Compared with doctors' estimated discharge dates, the predictive models:
o: have higher AUC, identify more discharges, and are more precise
have higher AUC but lower precision
match doctors' AUC but run faster
beat doctors on recall but lose on precision
quiz.e: All three metrics improve: AUC +0.18 to +0.21, discharges detected +1% to +16%, precision +10% to +12%. There is no recall/precision trade-off in the reported results.

quiz.q: In the 24-hour intensity results (MAE in knots), which model has the lowest error in the Eastern Pacific?
o: Deep Learning + Multimodal framework (10.3)
HWRF, best NHC dynamical model (10.6)
Deep Learning only (10.7)
Decay-SHIPS, best NHC statistical model (11.7)
quiz.e: In the Eastern Pacific the multimodal model's 10.3 beats HWRF's 10.6. HWRF is best only in the North Atlantic (9.7).

quiz.q: What does the calibration slide for the Hartford models establish?
o: Predicted probabilities closely match observed frequencies
Every hospital has AUC above 0.9
The model ranks patients in the right order
All 7 hospitals get identical predictions
quiz.e: Calibration means a predicted 0.6 really happens about 60% of the time, which is what lets fixed thresholds like 0.5 work. Ranking quality is AUC, a different property.

quiz.q: Which pipeline matches how HAIM builds a prediction from a patient's notes, ECG report, X-ray and lab events?
o: Turn each modality into features (text via ClinicalBERT/BioBERT, images via vision models), combine them into one patient representation, then train a predictor
Train one transformer end to end on raw pixels and raw text
Caption the images as text and use only a language model
Train one model per modality and keep the most confident prediction
quiz.e: HAIM extracts per-modality embeddings and fuses them into a unified patient representation that feeds the prediction model. Picking the most confident single-modality model would not use the modalities jointly.

quiz.q: 15 units serve 49,424 patients a year. LOS falls 0.67 days, the new average LOS is 4.98 days, and 50% of freed beds are backfilled. About how many extra patients a year?
o: About 3,325
About 6,649
About 16,557
About 33,114
quiz.e: 49,424 x 0.67 = 33,114 patient-days; / 4.98 = 6,649 patients' worth of beds; x 0.5 = 3,325. 16,557 halves the patient-days but skips dividing by LOS; 6,649 ignores the backfill share.

quiz.q: With about 3,325 extra patients a year at a contribution margin of $10,796 each, what is the annual CM increase, and what is the full-integration target once the 12 control units add $14.94M?
o: About $35.9M; about $50.8M
About $35.9M; about $71.8M
About $50.8M; about $65.7M
About $3.6M; about $18.5M
quiz.e: 3,325 x $10,796 = $35.9M, and $35.9M + $14.94M = $50.8M, matching the slide. $71.8M wrongly doubles the treatment figure.

quiz.q: North Atlantic, 24-hour intensity MAE: deep learning only is 11.4 kt, multimodal is 10.4 kt, and HWRF is 9.7 kt. Which statement is correct?
o: Multimodal cuts MAE about 8.8% vs deep learning only, but HWRF is still better there
Multimodal cuts MAE about 8.8% and beats every NHC model there
Multimodal cuts MAE about 9.6% vs deep learning only, and beats HWRF
Multimodal and HWRF tie in the North Atlantic
quiz.e: (11.4 - 10.4)/11.4 = 8.8%; 9.6% wrongly divides by 10.4. HWRF's 9.7 < 10.4, so the multimodal model is competitive but not best in this basin.

quiz.q: What is the main threat to the validity of the 0.67-day LOS effect, given how the slide says it was computed?
o: Treatment and control units might not have followed parallel trends, and the analysis is only preliminary
Too few patients to estimate any effect
The models are poorly calibrated
AUC at the deployed hospitals is below 0.7
quiz.e: The slide states the estimate assumes parallel trends and calls the analysis preliminary, with more rigorous work ongoing. Calibration and AUC are reported as good and concern prediction quality, not causal impact.

written.q: Describe the HAIM framework end to end: which modalities it uses, how each becomes features, what it predicts on MIMIC-IV, and what evidence shows multimodality helps. Name one reason to be careful about generalizing the results.
written.m: HAIM (Holistic AI in Medicine) combines notes, chest X-rays, ECGs, admissions information and chart/lab/procedure events into a unified patient representation. Unstructured text (clinical notes, ECG reports) and tabular event strings written as text (TabText) are embedded with ClinicalBERT/BioBERT into 768-element vectors; images go through vision models; the resulting features are fused and fed to a predictive model. On 34,537 MIMIC-IV emergency-ICU records from Beth Israel Deaconess it predicts mortality at discharge, 10 chest diagnoses, and discharge within 48 hours. Evidence: HAIM beats single-modality models by 11-33% (mortality), 6-22% (diagnosis) and 8-20% (LOS), and tabular + TabText beats tabular alone on every target (e.g., Enter ICU 48hr +9.73%). Caution: the data come from a single medical center, so performance elsewhere has to be checked, as the Hartford deployment does hospital by hospital.
k: Lists modalities: notes, X-rays, ECG, admissions, chart/lab/procedure events
Text embedded via ClinicalBERT/BioBERT into 768-dim vectors; TabText idea
Unified patient representation feeding a predictor

written.q: A hospital system asks you to estimate the annual financial value of deploying the discharge-prediction model in 15 units. Using the lecture's figures, lay out the calculation chain step by step and list the assumptions each step relies on.
written.m: Step 1, impact on LOS: 0.67-day reduction, estimated by comparing 15 fully deployed units with 12 not fully deployed units under a parallel-trend assumption (preliminary). Step 2, patient-days saved: 49,424 patients/yr x 0.67 = 33,114 days. Step 3, capacity: 33,114 / 4.98 (new average LOS) = 6,649 patients' worth of bed capacity. Step 4, backfill: only 50% of freed beds are refilled, so 3,325 extra patients. Step 5, value: 3,325 x $10,796 contribution margin = about $35.9M a year. Extending to the 12 control units adds $14.9M, for a $50.8M target. Assumptions: the 0.67-day effect is causal (parallel trends hold) and persists; the new LOS is 4.98 days; demand exists to backfill 50% of freed beds; added patients earn the average CM; the effect carries over to the control units.
k: Correct chain: patients x 0.67 / 4.98 x 50% x CM
Causal assumption: parallel trends / preliminary estimate
